channel.title: Nature Communications
channel.description:
Nature Communications is an open access, multidisciplinary journal dedicated to publishing high-quality research in all areas of the biological, health, physical, chemical and Earth sciences. Papers published by the journal aim to represent important advances of significance to specialists within each field.

We are committed to providing an efficient service for both authors and readers. Our team of independent editors make rapid and fair publication decisions. Prompt dissemination of accepted papers to a wide readership and beyond is achieved through a programme of continuous online publication.

item.title: Transport evidence for the orbital Nernst effect
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 22 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77878-2

The authors report experimental evidence of the orbital Nernst effect, demonstrating that heat can generate transverse orbital currents in a copper oxide film and opening new opportunities for heat-driven orbitronics.
item.dc:title: Transport evidence for the orbital Nernst effect

item.title: Strong acoustic meta-aerogels enabled by nanoconfined directional freezing and in-situ polymerization
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 22 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77972-5

This study reports cement-based meta-aerogels made by nanoconfined freezing-assisted in situ polymerization, with hierarchical pores that form resonant cavities for strong low-frequency absorption, mechanical robustness and scalable fabrication.

item.title: Structure and functional divergence of the non-canonical BoNT-like toxin PG1 and PG2
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 22 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77991-2

Here the authors characterise two botulinum-like toxins, PG1 and PG2. Their light chains cut a key protein in fruit flies; PG1 is toxic even without its heavy chain. PG1 has a distinct compact structure. These findings expand toxin knowledge and suggest potential as insecticides or research tools.
item.dc:title: Structure and functional divergence of the non-canonical BoNT-like toxin PG1 and PG2

item.title: Attractin-like protein 1 is an essential partner of MC4R to regulate body weight
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 22 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77897-z

The authors identified ATRNL1 as a key regulator of MC4R for appetite control. Loss of ATRNL1 or damaging ATRNL1 variants result in impaired MC4R signaling, increased food intake and promote weight gain. Mutations in Atrnl1 could contribute to obesity.
item.dc:title: Attractin-like protein 1 is an essential partner of MC4R to regulate body weight
